title: KV cache reconstruction and eviction resilience runbook
author: Marcus Lee
content:
Summary

This runbook describes how we detect and recover from KV cache loss caused by GPU node or pod evictions, and how to make the serving fleet resilient to repeated cold starts. It covers detection, automated remediation, manual reconstruction, Terraform/IaC recommendations for persistent seeding, CI/CD testing patterns, and post-incident actions. Intended audience: oncall SREs, serving-runtime engineers, and infra owners.

When to use this playbook

- Large-scale eviction event (>=10% of active GPU capacity) affecting model-serving pools.
- Cache hit rate drops below threshold for a model route for >5 minutes.
- Sudden increase in per-request latency and token cost correlated with bursts of cache misses.

Owner and stakeholders

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (pager: #serving-runtime-oncall)
- Secondary owner: eng-infra (pager: #infra-oncall)
- Observability and alerts: eng-platform
- Postmortem and follow-up: reliability-initiatives

SLOs and thresholds (operational)

- Cold-start tail latency (95th pct) for standard routes: target < 350ms; alert if > 550ms for 5m.
- Model KV cache hit rate: desired >= 92%; page if < 85% for 10m.
- Token cost per inference: monitor for > 2x baseline; create incident if sustained > 1h.

Detection: metrics & alerts

Key signals to check immediately:

- Metrics to query:
  - serving.kv_cache.hit_rate{model=<<name>>}
  - serving.request.latency_ms{route=<<route>>,percentile="p95"}
  - infra.gpu.evictions.count{region,zone}
  - serving.kv_cache.reconstruction_rate (new metric: reconstructions/min)

- Alerts to validate:
  1) KV-HIT-LOW: firing when kv_cache.hit_rate < 85% for 10m
  2) KV-COLD-TAIL: p95 latency > 550ms and token cost multiplier > 1.8 for 5m
  3) GPU-EVICT-SPIKE: gpu.evictions.count > 5 in 10m for same AZ/pool

First-response checklist (15 minutes)

1) Triage and scope
   - Confirm alert correlation (metrics + recent deploys).
   - Identify affected models and pools: run queries in Grafana/Metric Explorer for the last 30 minutes.
   - Post an incident note in #incidents and include initial impact estimate.

2) Short-term mitigation (automated and manual)
   - Ensure automatic fallback policies are enabled: route critical traffic to a pre-warmed variant (see routing policy: route-fallback:v1).
   - If fallback did not trigger, manually adjust routing policy via Console -> Routes -> Edit for the affected route to point to prewarmed model (steps below).
   - Increase autoscaler target for warm-pool (if available) with: kubectl patch hpa warm-pool -n serving --patch '{"spec": {"minReplicas": 8}}'

Automated cache reconstruction (recommended first-line)

We run a controlled reconstruction pipeline that replays representative prompt prefixes to refill KV cache without saturating GPUs. Use the replay service (internal: cache-seeder-service) which supports rate-limited seeding.

Automated run:

1) Trigger the cache-seeder with a target model and pool:
   curl -X POST https://cache-seeder.internal/api/v1/seed \n     -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SEEDER_TOKEN' \n     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \n     -d '{"model":"redwood-7b-v0", "pool":"eu-west-1-a", "rate_per_gpu":40, "duration_minutes":30 }'

2) Monitor: serving.kv_cache.fill_rate and GPU utilization. If GPU utilization > 70% for 5m, reduce rate_per_gpu by 50%.

3) Verify hit rate: expect incremental improvement in 10–20 minutes. Target: hit_rate >= 90% within 30–60 minutes for prewarmed models.

Manual reconstruction (when automated fails)

Use when reconstruction pipeline is unable to bootstrap (e.g., large model state mismatch):

1) Identify canonical prompt corpus for the model route (stored in s3://redwood-cache-seeds/<model>/canonical-prompts/).
2) Create a Kubernetes Job that mounts the canonical corpus and streams to the serving endpoint with controlled concurrency. Example manifest (abbreviated):

  apiVersion: batch/v1
  kind: Job
  metadata:
    name: kv-replay-{{model}}
    namespace: serving
  spec:
    template:
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: replayer
          image: gcr.io/redwood/cache-replayer:stable
          env:
            - name: TARGET_MODEL
              value: "redwood-7b-v0"
            - name: TARGET_ENDPOINT
              value: "https://serving.eu-west-1.redwood.internal"
            - name: CONCURRENCY
              value: "6"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: prompt-corpus
              mountPath: /data/corpus
        restartPolicy: Never
        volumes:
          - name: prompt-corpus
            persistentVolumeClaim:
              claimName: prompt-corpus-pvc
    backoffLimit: 2

3) Start at low concurrency (2–4) and ramp every 10 minutes while observing latency and utilization.

Terraform/IaC guidance (persistent seed and safe defaults)

Additions to Terraform modules for serving pools to reduce reconstruction blast radius:

- persistent_seed_volume (optional): a small read-only PVC that contains canonical prompt shards for that pool. Use a storage class with fast read performance (e.g., csi-local-ssd).
- seed-service-account: minimal IAM to pull seeds from S3/GCS and call internal APIs.
- module variables (example):
  - enable_seed_pvc: bool (default = true)
  - seed_pvc_size_gb: number (default = 10)
  - seed_rate_limit_per_gpu: number (default = 50)

Add example to tenant-serving module variables.tf:

variable "enable_seed_pvc" {
  description = "Mount read-only seed corpus for fast cache reconstruction"
  type        = bool
  default     = true
}

CI/CD and build verification patterns

We validate that runtime changes (kernel updates, mixed-precision kernels) do not regress cache reconstruction or increase cold-start cost:

- Canary test job: run cache-seed replay against canary images in CI with a production-like corpus and assert: p95 latency delta < 15% and cache-fill-time < defined threshold.
- Automated regression harness (nightly): deploy new runtime image to a shadow pool and run the replay pipeline; fail CI if hit-rate after 30m < 88%.
- Add unit tests for cache serialization/deserialization with Terraform-preserved seed versioning.

Operational Play: rollback and kernel gates

- If cache reconstruction fails AND latency/cost exceeds thresholds, trigger rollback of the last runtime/image change using the standard canary rollback play (Console -> Releases -> rollback).
- If kernel changes are suspected (mixed-precision kernel rollout), halt further kernel canaries and open a focused incident with runtime/kernel owners.

Post-incident and hardening actions

- Collect artifacts: Grafana dashboards, cache-seeder logs, Kubernetes events, kernel logs, and cache serialization dumps saved to s3://redwood-incident-artifacts/<incident-id>/
- Run a runbook retrospective with owners and add follow-up tasks to the reliability board (examples: increase seed PVC replication, expand canonical corpus coverage by 20%, tune seed rate limiter).

Playbook for small recurring evictions

If evictions are frequent but low-volume (1–3 nodes per day):

1) Increase warm-pool min replicas in the affected region by +2 and enable staggered draining.
2) Enable longer PV attachment grace for seed PVCs (mountPropagation if supported) so copies persist across transient failures.
3) Schedule a maintenance task: migrate high-cost models to more stable AZs or dedicated-pools (procedure described below).

Maintenance procedure: migrate a model to a dedicated pool

1) Create a new dedicated pool via Terraform:
   tf apply -target=module.model_pool["redwood-7b-dedicated"]
2) Promote the pool to receive live traffic in canary mode for 10–20% of traffic.
3) Run cache-seeder against the new pool and verify hit_rate >= 90% before increasing traffic share.

Diagnostics checklist (for engineers)

- Check host node dmesg/journald for OOMs or GPU driver resets.
- Inspect kubelet eviction logs: kubectl get events -n serving --field-selector reason=Evicted
- Confirm PV lifecycle: kubectl get pvc -n serving prompt-corpus-pvc -o yaml
- Validate cache serializer versions and model compatibility: serving-runtime exposes /internal/cache/version

Telemetry and dashboards to add (if missing)

- Per-model KV cache hit-rate heatmap by region/pool.
- Reconstruction job success rate and average time-to-90%-hit.
- Seed-service queue length and rate-limiter fallback events.

Runbook play examples (quick commands)

- Trigger automated seed for model:
  $ export SEEDER_TOKEN=$(vault read -field=token secret/infra/cache-seeder)
  $ curl -X POST https://cache-seeder.internal/api/v1/seed \n      -H "Authorization: Bearer $SEEDER_TOKEN" \n      -d '{"model":"redwood-7b-v0","pool":"us-west-2-b","rate_per_gpu":30,"duration_minutes":45}'

- Check reconstruction job status:
  $ kubectl get jobs -n serving | grep kv-replay
  $ kubectl logs job/kv-replay-redwood-7b-v0 -n serving --follow

Escalation matrix

- 0–15m: oncall SRE (pager: #serving-runtime-oncall)
- 15–60m: add eng-infra lead and runtime owner to incident channel
- >60m or customer-impacting: page head of eng-infra and Cx ops; open SEV-1 ticket and notify execs per incident policy

Appendix: seed corpus layout and retention

- Location: s3://redwood-cache-seeds/<model>/shard-<n>.jsonl
- Format: JSONL, one prompt per line, fields: {"prompt_id":"<id>", "prefix":"<text>", "metadata":{"route":"<route>"}}
- Retention policy: rotate canonical shards quarterly; keep last 4 rotations.
